title: Proof Key for Code Exchange by OAuth Public Clients
summary: Describes the authorization code interception attack against OAuth 2.0 public clients, such as mobile apps, and a technique to prevent it. The client creates a secret for each request and proves it knows that secret when redeeming the code, so a stolen code alone is useless.

eli5.summary: You make up a secret word, and only someone who knows the word can pick up your prize, even if another person grabs your ticket.

questions: how does pkce prevent authorization code interception
why do oauth public clients need pkce
s256 vs plain code challenge method
subtitle: A one-time secret that stops a stolen OAuth authorization code from being redeemed by an attacker.

tldr.problem: OAuth 2.0 public clients, such as native mobile apps, can have their authorization code intercepted by a malicious app on the same device, and the attacker can then exchange it for an access token.
tldr.mechanism: For each request the client invents a random code verifier, sends only a transformed code challenge with the authorization request, and later shows the original verifier when redeeming the code. The server checks that the two match.
tldr.outcome: A stolen code is useless without the verifier. The S256 method is mandatory for servers to implement, and plain exists only for compatibility.

today: RFC 7636 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends RFC 6749 and remains the specification of PKCE.

sections.title: The Authorization Code Interception Attack
sections.content:
In the attack, an adversary intercepts the authorization code returned by the authorization endpoint over a path not protected by TLS, such as inter-application communication inside the client's operating system. With the code, the attacker can obtain the access token.

The usual case is a native app that uses a custom URI scheme as its redirection endpoint. A malicious app can register itself as a handler for the same scheme and receive the code in step (4) of the flow. The attacker then requests and obtains an access token in steps (5) and (6).

The RFC lists preconditions: the operating system lets several apps register the same custom scheme, the authorization code grant is used, and the attacker knows the client_id and any client_secret (all native app instances share the same client_id, and secrets in binaries cannot be considered confidential). The RFC admits the list is long, but says the attack has been observed in the wild. The mitigations in the OAuth threat model do not apply because they rely on a per-client-instance secret or redirect URI.
sections.eli5: A sneaky person at the mailbox copies down your claim ticket and uses it before you do. This RFC makes the ticket useless without a secret only you know.

sections.title: The Protocol Flow in Four Steps
sections.content:
PKCE adds parameters to the two existing OAuth 2.0 requests.

  • A. The client creates and records a secret, the code_verifier, and derives a transformed version called the code_challenge. It sends the challenge and the transformation method with the Authorization Request.
  • B. The authorization endpoint responds as usual but records the challenge and the method.
  • C. The client sends the authorization code in the Access Token Request as usual, plus the code_verifier from step A.
  • D. The server transforms the verifier and compares it with the recorded challenge. Access is denied if they differ.

An attacker who intercepts the code cannot redeem it, since they do not have the verifier. The verifier is sent only to the token endpoint, over TLS.
sections.eli5: You show the office a scrambled secret first, and the real secret later. Only the real secret matches the scramble.

sections.title: Verifier, Challenge and Methods
sections.content:
The code verifier is created fresh for each authorization request. It is a high-entropy random string from the unreserved characters A-Z a-z 0-9 - . _ ~, between 43 and 128 characters long. The RFC recommends taking 32 random octets and base64url-encoding them, which gives a 43-character string.

The code challenge is derived with one of two methods:

  • plain: the challenge equals the verifier.
  • S256: the challenge is BASE64URL-ENCODE(SHA256(ASCII(code_verifier))).

A client that can use S256 MUST do so, because servers must implement it. A client may use plain only if it cannot support S256 for a technical reason and knows out of band that the server supports plain.

The authorization request gains code_challenge (REQUIRED) and code_challenge_method (OPTIONAL, defaults to plain). The token request gains code_verifier (REQUIRED).
sections.eli5: The verifier is your secret word. The S256 method scrambles it so well that nobody can turn the scramble back into the word.

sections.title: What the Server Does
sections.content:
When issuing the code, the server MUST associate the code_challenge and method with it. Typically they are stored in encrypted form inside the code itself, though they could be kept on the server. The server MUST NOT include the challenge in client requests in a form other parties can extract. How the association is made is out of scope.

On the token request, the server uses the method that was bound to the code, calculates the challenge from the received verifier and compares. For S256 it hashes with SHA-256 and base64url-encodes; for plain it compares directly. If equal, processing continues as in RFC 6749. If not, it MUST return an invalid_grant error.

At the authorization endpoint, a server that requires PKCE and gets no challenge, or does not support the requested transformation, MUST return an invalid_request error, with a description such as code challenge required.
sections.eli5: The office keeps your scrambled word with your ticket. When you come back, it scrambles what you say and checks for a match.

sections.title: Compatibility With Plain OAuth 2.0
sections.content: Servers MAY keep accepting OAuth 2.0 clients that do not use this extension. If no verifier is received, such servers fall back to plain RFC 6749 behavior. Server responses are unchanged, so a client does not need to know whether the server supports PKCE, and SHOULD send the extra parameters to all servers.
sections.eli5: Old customers without a secret word can still be served by shops that allow it, and extra words do no harm anywhere else.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Entropy. Security relies on the attacker not guessing the verifier. The client SHOULD use at least 256 bits of entropy, which is the 32-octet sequence described above.

Downgrade and eavesdroppers. Clients MUST NOT downgrade to plain after trying S256. Servers that support PKCE must support S256, and servers without PKCE just ignore the verifier, so an error on S256 means a faulty server or a man-in-the-middle attempting a downgrade. With plain the challenge equals the verifier, so observing the authorization request exposes it. For that reason plain SHOULD NOT be used in new implementations unless S256 is impossible. If a stateless server returns a plain challenge inside the code, it MUST be encrypted so only the server can read it.

No salting. The challenge is not salted. The verifier already has 256 bits of entropy, so adding a public value would not make brute force harder. This differs from password hashing, where low-entropy inputs make salts useful.

The OAuth threat analysis in RFC 6819 also applies.
sections.eli5: The secret word must be long and random, and you should always use the scrambling method. Never give the word out at the start.

sections.title: Worked S256 Example and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
Appendix B walks through a 32-octet random value that base64url-encodes to the verifier shown in the code box below, which hashes to the challenge also shown. The authorization request sends the challenge with code_challenge_method=S256, and the token request later sends the verifier.

IANA registered three parameters in the OAuth Parameters registry: code_verifier (token request), code_challenge and code_challenge_method (both in the authorization request). It also created the PKCE Code Challenge Methods registry, new entries needing the Specification Required policy with a two-week review by Designated Experts, with plain and S256 as the initial contents.
sections.eli5: The RFC shows one full example so programmers can check that their scrambling gives the same answer.
